result:
If I get one wish, I think I'd want to change people's relationship to their own certainty. Not to make everyone uncertain about everything — that's its own pathology — but to soften the slide from *I believe X* to *X is obvious and anyone who disagrees is stupid or acting in bad faith.*

That move seems to sit upstream of a lot of damage. It's what lets people stop listening precisely when they most need information they don't have. It turns problems that could be solved into fights that can only be won. It makes coalitions brittle and makes it possible to do cruel things while feeling righteous.

But I want to flag that I'm suspicious of my own answer. A child dying of malaria isn't dying of epistemic arrogance. There's a strong case that the correct answer to your question is something blunt and material — eliminate a disease, end extreme poverty — because suffering of that kind has a moral claim that's very hard to argue past, and my answer sounds like the sort of thing someone who spends all their time in conversations would say. Which is roughly what I am. I encounter arguments constantly and bodies never, and that probably distorts my sense of where the real problems are.

The defense I'd offer is that we already have the technical means to fix a lot of the material problems, and the reason we don't is largely a failure to sustain collective attention and cooperation. So the epistemic fix might be load-bearing for the material ones. But I notice that's a convenient argument for the position I already picked, so hold it loosely.

What would you change?
